title: Pancho the brave dog
summary: Pancho discovers that being brave doesn't mean having no fear, but moving forward anyway.

scenes.text: Pancho was a small puppy with brown fur and white spots, long floppy ears, and a tail that wagged like a metronome whenever he was happy. He lived in a small house with his family, in a quiet neighborhood full of trees. The house had a garden with flowers of every color: red, yellow, purple, white. Pancho was sweet and playful, he loved chasing balls and tumbling in the grass. All the neighbors knew him and smiled when they saw him on his walks. But Pancho had a secret no one knew, not his family, not his friends at the park, not even the neighbor's cat: he was very, very afraid of storms. Every time the sky turned gray, high above you could hear the thunder. Then something began to jump inside his chest like a frightened rabbit: his heart. Bumbumbumbum. His ears would droop even more and his tail would tuck between his legs. He would run to hide under his human's bed, in the darkest corner, and stay there very still, very still, with his paws covering his ears, waiting for all that ugly noise to pass.

One October night, a huge storm fell over the neighborhood. It started with a sky that grew darker and darker, then some far-away lightning, and suddenly it broke loose. The rain hit the roof like a thousand small drums, and the windows shook with every clap of thunder. The lightning lit up the walls like giant flashes. Pancho, faithful to his routine, ran to hide under the bed, trembling. "Please let it stop, please let it stop," he thought with his eyes squeezed shut. But in a short pause in the storm, Pancho heard something different. Something that wasn't rain, or wind, or storm. It was a thin, sharp, frightened sound. Meow! Meowww! Meowwwww! Pancho poked his head out from under the blankets and listened carefully. Yes, there it was again: somewhere out there someone was meowing. It was a lost kitten, somewhere in the garden, in the rain, wet and alone, calling for its mom. Pancho felt his heart squeeze with sadness, as if someone were giving him a very tight hug from inside.

Pancho was still trembling with fear. The storm hadn't stopped; just the opposite, it seemed worse and worse. But something inside him, a small and firm voice, said: "Pancho, you have to help." The little dog opened his eyes. He looked toward the hallway. He swallowed hard. "I can't," he thought at first. "Yes you can," answered the voice. Pancho took a deep breath, once, twice. He came out of his hiding spot step by step, with his paws a little wobbly. He crossed the living room, passed the couch, and reached the garden door. He pushed it with his snout, click, and peeked out. The rain soaked his fur in a second, the thunder roared above, the drops fell into his eyes. But Pancho kept walking, sniffing the air to find the kitten. Soaking wet and curled up in a ball, he found it under a bush. Then he gathered all his courage and barked. "I'm here! Don't be scared!" He came closer slowly, picked it up gently with his mouth, taking great care not to hurt it, and carried it home. He brought his favorite towel, the softest one, and helped it dry off.

The kitten, now feeling dry and warm, slowly stopped trembling. Its green eyes calmed down. It began to purr softly, a purr of gratitude, prrr, prrr, prrr. Pancho curled up next to the kitten and hugged it with his furry paws, like a stuffed animal. The two of them stayed like that, close together, on Pancho's bed, listening to the storm from inside. Pancho rested his ear against its chest and listened to the heartbeat. Outside the rain kept falling and the thunder kept roaring, but inside there was warmth, there was company, there was safety. And suddenly Pancho realized something important: he wasn't scared anymore. Well, yes, he was scared, but a different kind of scared, smaller, because something bigger than fear had grown inside him: love. That night Pancho learned a secret he would remember forever: being brave doesn't mean having no fear. Being brave means having fear and, even so, going out to help others. While the rain far outside lulled them like a lullaby, the two friends fell asleep.
